title: SYSK Selects: How Chaos Theory Changed the Universe
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the 2016 episode on chaos theory. Josh introduces it as a favorite and the hosts trace how determinism and Newtonian mechanics led to the discovery of chaos. Topics include Laplace-style determinism, Newton's laws, Poincaré's three-body (N-body) problem and King Oscar II prize, Edward Lorenz's accidental discovery with a weather model on a Royal McBee computer and the butterfly effect, the Lorenz strange attractor and the town/grocery store analogy, Stephen Smale's horseshoe map, and Robert May's logistic map with James Yorke's 1975 paper "Period Three Implies Chaos" that coined the term. The episode closes with a listener mail segment and sign-off, with a few digressions into movies (Jurassic Park, Event Horizon, Forrest Gump) and a mention of the fractals episode.

segments.title: Selects intro and chaos movie banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces this SYSK Selects pick as a favorite. The hosts banter about Event Horizon and the Jurassic Park chaos scene, and note that the popular meaning of chaos is misleading.

segments.title: Determinism and Newtonian science
segments.summary: The hosts describe the shift from a theistic worldview to the scientific revolution, Descartes' cause and effect, and Newton's laws. They explain determinism: with exact measurements, a system's future can be predicted, illustrated with a pool table.

segments.title: Overconfidence in prediction and measurement precision
segments.summary: Hosts discuss science's confidence in prediction, the 1846 prediction of Neptune, and the 19th and 20th century push for more precise instruments. They note that measurement error limits predictions.

segments.title: Poincaré and the three-body problem
segments.summary: King Oscar II offered a prize for proving the stability of the solar system. Henri Poincaré studied the three-body (N-body) problem and found that tiny differences in initial conditions produce wildly different outcomes, so the proof was impossible and determinism was undermined.

segments.title: Lorenz and the Royal McBee weather model
segments.summary: Edward Lorenz, a meteorologist and mathematician, was motivated by failed weather forecasting and the 1962 Ash Wednesday and Big Blow storms. Using a Royal McBee computer, he ran a twelve-variable weather model and found that rounding inputs from three to six decimal places produced a very different result.

segments.title: Lorenz attractor and the butterfly effect
segments.summary: Lorenz simplified his model to three equations describing a rolling convection current. Graphed in three dimensions, the path never repeated, producing the Lorenz attractor. His 1972 talk title, about a butterfly in Brazil setting off a tornado in Texas, gave the butterfly effect its name.

segments.title: Attractors explained with a town analogy
segments.summary: Using a small-town analogy with a grocery store and factory, the hosts explain equilibrium as an attractor and a strange attractor as a system that keeps searching for equilibrium with periods of stability.

segments.title: Smale horseshoe, Robert May, and the coining of chaos
segments.summary: Stephen Smale's horseshoe map shows how nearby points diverge. Robert May's logistic difference equation showed population behavior splitting into cycles and then chaos. With James Yorke, he published 'Period Three Implies Chaos' in 1975, which introduced the word chaos.

segments.title: Chaos as a new understanding of the universe and forecasting
segments.summary: Chaos took off in the 1980s and 1990s, faded from the spotlight, but remained a field. The hosts describe modern data-driven modeling and explain why ten-day forecasts and extinction predictions can miss.

segments.title: Listener mail from John
segments.summary: A listener named John, deployed overseas, writes that the show helps on drives and asks for a shout-out to his girlfriend Rachel, who finds talk radio gives her a headache.
